title: Facial color patterns and intraspecific facial signaling complexity in domesticated cats (Felis silvestris catus)
short_title: Facial color patterns and facial signaling complexity in domestic cats
abstract: Recent studies have revealed an inverse relationship between the complexity of facial color patterns and the intricacy of facial signaling. As facial color patterns become more elaborate, facial signaling complexity de-creases, because intricate colors may distract from and hinder the perception of subtle facial muscle movements. Recent studies have confirmed this trade-off across multiple primate species and have also identified it within domesticated dogs. The goal of our current study was to assess whether such a trade-off exists among other domesticated species, such as cats (Felis silvestris catus). Data were collected at a cat café, including 53 adult domestic shorthairs that vary extensively in their fur colors and patterns. We constructed a facial color pattern complexity scoring rubric that is consistent with previously published work. This rubric was implemented using automated approaches (Google Gemini) to ensure consistency in the evaluation of cat faces. We utilized sys-tematic and standardized methods to study cat facial muscle movements (catFACS). We assessed and oper-ationalized the complexity of facial signaling based on three criteria: (1) the number of distinct types of facial muscle movements produced by each cat (AU Type); (2) the number of unique combinations of facial muscle movements produced by each cat (AU Combo); and (3) the total number of discrete facial muscle movements that typically make up each cat's facial signals (AU Length). Ordinal regressions were used to evaluate the relationship between our independent (facial color pattern complexity scores) and dependent (AU Type, AU Combo, AU Length) variables. Our results indicate that there are no statistically significant differences in our three measures of facial signaling complexity based on cat facial color pattern complexity scores. Further research with other felids, both domestic and wild, is necessary to explore these relationships more thoroughly.
summary: Earlier work in primates and dogs found that animals with more elaborate facial color patterns tend to use simpler facial expressions, because intricate colors can hide subtle muscle movements. We tested this trade-off in 53 adult domestic shorthair cats at a cat cafe, scoring facial color complexity with an automated rubric (Google Gemini) and coding facial movements with the standardized catFACS system. We found no statistically significant differences in three measures of facial signaling complexity based on color pattern complexity.
key_findings: Data came from 53 adult domestic shorthair cats at a cat cafe, with widely varying fur colors and patterns.
Signaling complexity was measured by the number of movement types, unique movement combinations and movements per facial signal.
None of the three signaling complexity measures differed significantly with facial color pattern complexity scores.
Further research with other felids, both domestic and wild, is needed to explore these relationships.
